newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem blames Argentine job protests on tax evasion.
newsitem.headline: Menem blames Argentine job protests on tax evasion.

text.p: President Carlos Menem on Wednesday blamed tax dodgers and the "black" economy for roadblocks spreading through Argentine provinces in protest of unemployment and poverty.

With 10 barricades on roads in the poor northwestern province of Jujuy and three in the central province of Cordoba, Menem tried to shift the blame for unemployment, which has risen to 17.3 percent from 6 percent when he came to power in 1989.

"The day we can legalise the situation of more than 5 million people working in the 'black' economy, unemployment in Argentina will fall below 10 percent," the Peronist leader told Argentine reporters accompanying him to Germany.

Menem also quoted World Bank figures showing poverty in Argentina has fallen to 18 percent from 38 percent in 1989, and said he would gladly reduce the value added tax on basic goods to help the poor -- if business people started paying taxes.

His government, widely praised for stabilising the economy and achieving zero inflation, has been warned in the past week by the Catholic Church and the International Monetary Fund about the dangers of neglecting the poor and jobless.

Protests turned violent last week, with more than 100 people hurt in clashes between police and unemployed sugar workers in shanty towns in Jujuy, skirmishes in the city of La Plata and riots aimed at a privatisation in Mendoza.

There was violence in an earlier roadblock by jobless oilworkers in the province of Neuquen. Teachers were on a hunger strike over the education budget and students took to the streets in Buenos Aires on Wednesday demanding more cash and action on jobs.

But Menem played down the scale of protests, saying "out of 600 municipalities we only have problems in ... just one province," adding that riots were fermented by opposition rivals ahead of October's mid-term elections in Congress.
"Some might be trying to provoke some sort of repression from the province, security forces or the national government. But we are not going to play ball," Menem said.

State workers led by hardline unionist Carlos "the Dog" Santillan struck for a second day in Jujuy in sympathy with the pickets. Santillan told strikers: "We need deep changes in policy on who has to pay for the crisis in this province."
Unemployment in some Jujuy towns was as high as 37 percent. Along with neighbouring Salta and two other provinces, it has missed out on the "economic miracle" and output has actually shrunk.

But Menem said, "Argentina is growing, we live in peace and and these problems are logical in a country which is changing. "All this is not going to make us turn from the path we chose in 1989, with excellent results for the country."
